title: A Constitution for a Game
bigQuestion: Who writes the rules of a league, and whose interests do those written rules protect?

story.title: A Car Showroom in Canton
story.kicker: In September 1920 team owners met among new cars in Ohio and founded a football league.
paragraphs: It is September 17, 1920, in Canton, Ohio. A car dealer named Ralph Hay sells Hupmobiles here. He also runs the Canton Bulldogs, a professional football team. Tonight men from about a dozen teams crowd into his showroom. There are not enough chairs, so some sit on the running boards of the cars.

Professional football is messy in 1920. Teams steal each other's players in the middle of a season. Some clubs pay college students to play under fake names. Crowds are small, and money is short. The men in the room want order, and they want it to protect their teams.

By the end of the night they have formed the American Professional Football Association. They choose Jim Thorpe, the most famous athlete in the room, as its president. Two years later the association will rename itself the National Football League.

No players vote in the showroom. The owners write the league's first rules for themselves. Over the next century, players will organize, sue and bargain to gain a voice in rules they did not write. The showroom meeting shows who held the pen at the start.
story.think: Why might owners and players want different rules in the same league?

lessons.title: Cricket's Laws of 1744
lessons.mainIdea: Cricket had a written code by 1744, and London's Marylebone Cricket Club became the keeper of its laws after 1787.
reading: The oldest known written laws of cricket date from 1744. Gentlemen of several clubs agreed to them in London. Men were betting large sums on matches, and bets needed clear rules to settle them. The code fixed things such as the length of the pitch, 22 yards, which cricket still uses.

In 1787 a group of wealthy players founded the *Marylebone Cricket Club*, or MCC. It played at a ground laid out by Thomas Lord, a name kept by Lord's Cricket Ground today. In 1788 the MCC issued its own revised laws. Other clubs began to follow them, so a private club became the game's lawmaker.

No government gave the MCC this power. It gained *authority*, the accepted right to make rules, because clubs chose to copy its code. The MCC kept writing the Laws of Cricket for more than two centuries. It still holds the copyright to them, while the International Cricket Council runs world competitions.

words.d: a private London club, founded in 1787, that became the keeper of the Laws of Cricket
the accepted right to make rules and decide disputes
a written set of rules that people agree to follow

lessons.title: The Jockey Club at Newmarket
lessons.mainIdea: The Jockey Club, formed around 1750, grew from a social club into the body that governed British horse racing.
reading: Newmarket is a town in eastern England where horses have raced since the 1600s. King Charles II raced and watched there. Around 1750 a group of wealthy men who owned racehorses formed the *Jockey Club*. At first it was a social club for owners who met to dine and talk.

Owners had money riding on fair results. The club began to settle disputes over races at Newmarket. Over time other courses asked it to judge their disputes too. Its rules on races, the weights horses carried and the horses themselves spread across Britain.

The club's strongest tool was the power to *warn off*. A person who was warned off was banned from racecourses under the club's rules. For about two centuries the Jockey Club governed British racing. In 2006 a separate authority took over that job, now called the British Horseracing Authority.

words.d: a club of racehorse owners formed around 1750 at Newmarket that came to govern British horse racing
to ban a person from racecourses, the Jockey Club's strongest punishment
a disagreement that someone must decide, such as who truly won a race

check.why: Warning off was a ban from racecourses, the club's strongest tool.

lessons.title: Twelve Clubs in 1888
lessons.mainIdea: In 1888 twelve English clubs formed the Football League, a new kind of body built around a fixed schedule and shared gate money.
reading: By the 1880s English soccer clubs were paying players, and they needed steady crowds to pay wages. Many games were friendlies, arranged one at a time, and some were cancelled. In March 1888 William McGregor of Aston Villa wrote to other clubs. He proposed a fixed list of home and away matches each season.

Twelve clubs formed the *Football League* in 1888. Six came from Lancashire and six from the Midlands. The Football Association, founded in 1863, still wrote the Laws of the Game. The League was different: it ran a season-long competition as a business partnership of clubs.

In the 1890s the League added a Second Division. Clubs then moved up by *promotion* and down by *relegation* based on results. This made English soccer an open system, in which any club could climb. Most major American leagues instead became closed systems, where the same teams stay in no matter where they finish.

words.d: the English league formed by twelve clubs in 1888 to play a fixed season of matches
moving a club up to a higher division because of good results
moving a club down to a lower division because of poor results

lessons.title: The Black Sox and a Judge
lessons.mainIdea: After Chicago White Sox players were accused of fixing the 1919 World Series, owners gave a single commissioner broad power over baseball.
reading: The Chicago White Sox lost the 1919 World Series to the Cincinnati Reds. In 1920 a grand jury in Chicago looked into claims that gamblers paid White Sox players to lose. Eight players were charged. Newspapers soon called the disgraced team the *Black Sox*.

The owners feared fans would stop trusting the game. Until then baseball was run by a three-man National Commission. In November 1920 the owners chose Kenesaw Mountain Landis, a federal judge in Chicago, as the first *commissioner*. He took office in January 1921 and demanded nearly unchecked power as his price.

A Chicago jury found the eight players not guilty in August 1921. The next day Landis banned all eight from organized baseball for life anyway. His ruling showed that a league's private power could reach further than a court. Shoeless Joe Jackson, one of the eight, was never allowed back while he lived.

words.d: the nickname for the 1919 Chicago White Sox players accused of taking gamblers' money to lose the World Series
a single official chosen by a league's owners to govern the sport and punish wrongdoing
a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough evidence to charge someone with a crime

lessons.title: In the Best Interests
lessons.mainIdea: Baseball's commissioner can punish acts found to hurt the best interests of the game, a broad power used against Pete Rose in 1989.
reading: The 1921 agreement that hired Landis gave the commissioner power to act on anything he judged harmful to the *best interests of baseball*. The phrase was not defined. Its vagueness was its strength, since it let the commissioner punish acts no rule had listed. Club owners even promised not to take the commissioner to court.

Pete Rose holds the record for the most hits in major league history. In 1989 an investigation found that he had bet on baseball games, including games of the Cincinnati Reds, the team he managed. In August 1989 Rose signed an agreement with Commissioner Bart Giamatti. It placed him on baseball's permanently *ineligible* list.

In 1991 the Baseball Hall of Fame voted that people on that list could not be elected. So the league's private ruling also kept Rose off the Hall of Fame ballot. In May 2025 Commissioner Rob Manfred ruled that a ban ends when a person dies. That decision took Rose, who died in 2024, and Joe Jackson off the list.

words.d: the broad, undefined standard that lets baseball's commissioner punish acts harmful to the game
not allowed to take part, for example in a league or in an election to a hall of fame
a careful search for facts about what someone did

lessons.title: From President to Commissioner
lessons.mainIdea: Pro football's league began with a famous athlete as president in 1920 and created a commissioner's office in 1941.
reading: The American Professional Football Association formed in Canton, Ohio, in 1920. Its first president was Jim Thorpe, the Olympic champion and player for the Canton Bulldogs. Thorpe gave the league a famous name, but he ran it for only one year. In 1921 Joe Carr, an Ohio sports promoter, became president and served until his death in 1939.

In 1922 the association renamed itself the *National Football League*. Carr worked to stop teams from signing college players before their classes graduated. He also pushed teams to settle in larger cities. Small-town clubs from places such as Canton and Decatur, Illinois, gave way to city teams.

The Decatur Staleys, a founding team, moved to Chicago in 1921 and became the Chicago Bears in 1922. In 1941 the owners created the title of commissioner, following baseball's example. Elmer Layden, a former Notre Dame star and coach, was the first to hold it. The title said the league now wanted one strong *executive* over its clubs.

words.d: the name taken in 1922 by the American Professional Football Association, founded in Canton in 1920
a person who runs an organization and carries out its decisions
a person who organizes and sells sports events

lessons.title: Rugby Splits in 1895
lessons.mainIdea: In 1895 northern English rugby clubs broke away over pay for lost work time, splitting rugby into two codes.
reading: In the 1890s many rugby players in northern England worked in mills and mines. A Saturday match could cost them a day's pay. Northern clubs asked to pay players for this lost time, called *broken time*. The Rugby Football Union, based in the south and led by men of wealth, refused.

On August 29, 1895, twenty-two clubs met at the George Hotel in Huddersfield. They formed the Northern Rugby Football Union. It allowed broken-time payments. The Rugby Football Union then treated anyone who joined the northern body as a professional and banned them.

The northern game changed its own rules over the years and in 1922 took the name *rugby league*. The older game became known as rugby union. The split shows *amateurism* as a belief about social class. Men who did not need wages could afford the rule that no one should be paid.

words.d: pay to make up for wages a worker lost by leaving work to play
the rugby code that grew from the northern clubs that broke away in 1895
the belief and rule that athletes should not be paid to play

check.why: Twenty-two clubs met at the George Hotel in Huddersfield on August 29, 1895.

check.q: What does the rugby split show about amateurism?
choices: It was a belief tied to social class

check.why: The rule cost wage earners far more than wealthy players, so it worked as a class belief.

lessons.title: Tennis Opens Its Doors, 1968
lessons.mainIdea: In 1968 major tennis tournaments opened to professionals, ending a long split between amateur and paid players.
reading: For decades the major tennis championships, such as Wimbledon, admitted only amateurs. Top players who turned professional joined touring shows and were barred from the majors. Meanwhile some amateurs quietly took large expense payments. Critics called this hidden pay *shamateurism*.

In 1967 the All England Club, which runs Wimbledon, said it would open the tournament to professionals. The International Lawn Tennis Federation agreed in March 1968. In April 1968 the British Hard Court Championships in Bournemouth became the first *open* tournament. Wimbledon held its first open championship that summer.

The *Open Era* followed. Rod Laver, who had been barred from the majors as a professional, won the Grand Slam of all four major titles in 1969. Prize money became public and grew. The change ended a rule that had pushed paid players out of sight rather than out of the sport.

words.d: hidden payments to athletes who were officially amateurs
describing a tournament that admits both amateurs and professionals
the period of tennis since 1968, when major tournaments admit professionals

lessons.title: Rugby Union Turns Professional
lessons.mainIdea: In August 1995, exactly a century after the northern split, rugby union's world body dropped its amateur rule.
reading: Rugby union stayed officially amateur for most of the 1900s. Players who joined rugby league were often banned from union for life. By the 1990s top union players were earning money through jobs, gifts and sponsors arranged around the rule. The first Rugby World Cup in 1987 and television deals brought in large sums.

In 1995 South Africa hosted the Rugby World Cup. Media companies were offering to set up a paid competition. The *International Rugby Football Board*, the game's world governing body, met in Paris. On August 26, 1995, it declared rugby union an open game, in which players could be paid.

The date came almost exactly one hundred years after the Huddersfield meeting of 1895. The amateur rule that had split the sport was gone. Some older clubs struggled to pay wages, and professional *franchises* and club leagues grew. The world body later renamed itself World Rugby, in 2014.

words.d: the world governing body of rugby union, renamed World Rugby in 2014
a team that holds the right to play in a league, often owned as a business
an organization that writes the rules and runs official competition for a sport

lessons.title: A Draft Is Voted In
lessons.mainIdea: In 1935 NFL owners voted to create a draft, a rule that assigned college players to teams and took away their choice of employer.
reading: In the early 1930s rich NFL teams signed the best college players, and weak teams stayed weak. Bert Bell owned the Philadelphia Eagles, one of the struggling clubs. In 1935 he proposed a *draft*. Teams would take turns choosing college players, with the worst team choosing first.

The owners approved the plan, and the first draft was held in February 1936 in Philadelphia. The first pick was Jay Berwanger of the University of Chicago, who had won the first Heisman Trophy. Berwanger never played in the NFL. He took a job in business instead of accepting the pay that was offered.

The draft helped *competitive balance*, the idea that any team might win. It also meant a player could negotiate with only one team. The owners voted it in; the players had no vote. Other leagues later adopted drafts, and players' unions would bargain over them for decades.

words.d: a system in which teams take turns choosing new players, usually with the weakest team choosing first
the goal that teams in a league have similar chances to win
to talk with another side to reach an agreement, such as a contract

lessons.title: One Company or Thirty-Two
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a league is one business or many separate ones matters in court, as Major League Soccer's design and the 2010 American Needle case show.
reading: Major League Soccer was founded in 1995 and played its first season in 1996. It was built as a *single entity*. The league itself signed player contracts, and investors ran teams inside one company. Its founders hoped this would control costs after earlier American soccer leagues had failed.

In 1997 MLS players sued, claiming the design let the league hold down pay unfairly. A federal jury decided in 2000 that the players had not proved their case. The design survived. It shows that a league's *structure* is a choice written into its founding papers.

The NFL wanted similar protection. Its teams had given one company, Reebok, the sole right to make their caps. A cap maker called American Needle sued under *antitrust* law. In 2010 the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that NFL teams are separate businesses when they sell their logos, so antitrust law applies to them.

words.d: a league organized as one company that owns contracts, instead of a group of separate team businesses
the way an organization is built, including who owns what and who decides
laws that stop businesses from joining together to block competition

lessons.title: Wrigley's League of Women
lessons.mainIdea: The All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, founded in 1943 by Chicago's Philip K. Wrigley, wrote rules for how its players must look and act.
reading: In 1943 many male baseball players were serving in World War II. Philip K. Wrigley, owner of the Chicago Cubs and of the Wrigley chewing gum company, started a professional league for women. It became the *All-American Girls Professional Baseball League*. Teams played in Midwestern cities such as Rockford, Illinois, and Racine and Kenosha, Wisconsin.

The league had written rules about more than the game. Players wore short-skirted uniforms. They attended a *charm school* for lessons on makeup and manners. Rules banned short haircuts, and each team had chaperones who watched players off the field.

The league lasted until 1954 and gave hundreds of women paid careers in baseball. It did not sign Black players, even after Jackie Robinson joined the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947. The 1992 film A League of Their Own, about the Rockford Peaches, brought the league wider fame. Its rule book shows a league governing players' lives as well as their play.

words.d: a women's pro league founded in 1943 by Philip K. Wrigley that lasted until 1954
lessons in makeup, dress and manners that the league required its players to attend
an adult assigned to watch over and supervise players away from the game
